title: External resolver fallback exposes private tenant hostnames during peering failover
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: During a scheduled peering maintenance window we received multiple customer escalations (two Enterprise Dedicated tenants) reporting that internal service hostnames (svc.*.local) temporarily resolved to external IPs and, in several cases, DNS queries were forwarded to the global resolver instead of the tenant-local forwarder. Impact: potential disclosure of internal hostnames to external resolvers and intermittent cross-tenant resolution noise; customer-facing symptom: failed internal service discovery and spurious 403s when internal services attempted auth against tenant-scoped services. Scope: affected two Dedicated tenants in us-west-2 for ~13 minutes during a peering route withdraw/re-announce event.

Reproduction (investigation notes):
1) Start with Dedicated tenant A configured to use per-tenant DNS forwarder at 169.254.16.23 via peering route.
2) Trigger peering failover (simulated route withdraw) while heavy DNS traffic is present (burst of SRV/AAAA lookups from pods with short TTLs ~10s).
3) Observed behavior: egress datapath fell back to node-level resolver (global resolver at 10.0.0.2) because peering next-hop was temporarily missing; responses from 10.0.0.2 contained cached records for other tenants; those responses were cached in the node resolver and, after conntrack/SNAT rebind, were served to subsequent lookups from different tenants.

Root cause hypothesis: a race between route reprogramming and the per-tenant resolver affinity logic in the egress datapath. When the per-tenant route to the local DNS forwarder was withdrawn, the fallback path used the node/global resolver without clearing resolver-affinity state or segregated response caches. The node resolver caches (and the kernel-level DNS cache) were not namespace-aware in our current implementation, allowing stale/cross-tenant entries to be reused until TTL expiration.

Immediate mitigation taken:
- Ops: Reverted the peering change and forced immediate route reprogramming; this restored tenant-local forwarding within 90s for affected customers.
- Emergency policy: rolled out iptables rule on affected nodes to block outbound 53 to global resolver IP 10.0.0.2 from Dedicated tenant namespaces. This prevented further leakage while we worked on the fix. (Rollout: 14 nodes, done at 2026-03-10T14:22Z.)
- Customer comms: Notified the two impacted customers with timeline and mitigation steps; offering a post-incident call.

Proposed permanent fixes / plan:
1) Short-term patch (hotfix): update egress datapath to prefer per-tenant resolver when a previous resolver was configured and only fall back after a configurable grace period; clear per-tenant response cache entries when route/peering state changes. Target: runtime-1.23 patch release (hotfix-1.23.1).
2) Medium-term: make node resolver cache namespace-aware (segregate caches by tenant ID) and add invariant checks to prevent serving cached responses to requests from different tenant namespaces.
3) Long-term: add end-to-end tests that simulate peering withdraws and rapid resolver failovers; add tracing to DNS flows to detect fallback events in real-time and alert on cross-tenant cache hits.

Risks and notes:
- Hotfix involves changes to egress datapath and cache invalidation; must validate across Dedicated and Private (VPC) deployments to avoid performance regressions.
- Blocking global resolver 10.0.0.2 temporarily may impact non-dedicated workloads; we scoped rule to dedicated nodes only.

Success criteria:
- No DNS responses for tenant-internal hostnames are observed from external/global resolvers after peering changes in canary region for 48h.
- Automated tests covering peering withdraw -> resolver fallback pass in CI.

Postmortem / follow-up actions (to be tracked):
- Runbook updates: add explicit step to prevent global-resolver fallback during peering transitions; include timeline and thresholds.
- Dashboard: add metric for "resolver_fallback_events" and "cross_tenant_dns_cache_hits" with customer-impact alerting.
- Communication: schedule customer post-incident briefing and include remediation plan and timeline.
